questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the left forearm with a central black eschar surrounded by significant non-pitting edema. He had contact with cattle hides 5 days ago. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax from Bacillus anthracis presents as a painless papule → vesicle → eschar with surrounding non-pitting edema (malignant pustule). Contact with animal hides/wool is a classic exposure.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient develops multiple hyperkeratotic plaques on the dorsum of the hands and periungual area. KOH mount shows broad hyphae with chains of arthroconidia. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Tinea manuum presents with diffuse scaling on the palm/dorsum. KOH showing broad hyphae with arthroconidia indicates dermatophyte infection. Chromoblastomycosis shows sclerotic bodies (Medlar/copper pennies).

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with multiple shallow, painful ulcers on the labia with inguinal lymphadenopathy. The causative organism can be grown on chocolate agar with X and V factors. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) causes painful genital ulcers with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). H. ducreyi requires X factor (hemin) only for growth, distinguishing it from H. influenzae which needs both X and V.

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient on long-term steroid therapy develops skin lesions with a 'dimorphic' fungus on tissue biopsy showing large yeast cells with narrow-necked buds surrounded by a thick capsule. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Cryptococcus neoformans produces large yeast cells with a thick polysaccharide capsule, demonstrated by India ink stain. Narrow-necked (single) buds differentiate it from Blastomyces (broad-based buds). Common in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset fever, erythematous tender nodules on the trunk and extremities, and iridocyclitis. The nerve function is stable. This reaction is classified as:
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2) is an immune complex-mediated reaction occurring in lepromatous/borderline lepromatous leprosy. Features include tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic involvement (iridocyclitis, orchitis). Nerve function is typically not acutely impaired unlike Type 1.

questions.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly in the flexural areas. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense bullae (subepidermal), flexural distribution, and DIF showing linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ. Target antigens are BP180 and BP230. Pemphigus shows IgG in intercellular spaces (fishnet pattern).

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with Sjögren's syndrome develops a slowly enlarging sclerotic plaque with a lilac-colored border (lilac ring) around the wrist. Histopathology shows homogenized collagen in the dermis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Morphea (localized scleroderma) presents with indurated sclerotic plaques with an active lilac/violaceous border (inflammatory margin). Histopathology shows thickened, homogenized collagen bundles in the dermis. Unlike systemic sclerosis, it lacks systemic involvement.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on erythematous base on the genitalia with burning pain, preceded by tingling/itching for 2 days. The virus responsible can be differentiated from VZV by its ability to:
questions.exp: HSV-2 (genital herpes) causes recurrent genital vesicles with a prodrome. Unlike VZV (which follows a dermatomal pattern due to reactivation), HSV can cause non-dermatomal recurrences. Both form multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck smear) and cause latency in sensory ganglia.

questions.q: Psoriatic plaques with silvery scales, Auspitz sign, and candle grease sign are noted in a 30-year-old. The primary immunopathogenic mechanism involves:
questions.exp: Psoriasis is driven primarily by the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis. IL-23 from dendritic cells drives Th17 differentiation, producing IL-17A/F and IL-22, which stimulate keratinocyte hyperproliferation. This is the basis for biologics targeting IL-17 (secukinumab), IL-23 (guselkumab), and TNF.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient on immunosuppressive therapy develops painful hemorrhagic bullae, rapidly progressing necrosis with a black eschar on the thigh. Gram stain of wound discharge shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The most likely organism is:
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis Type II caused by MRSA presents with hemorrhagic bullae and rapid necrosis in immunocompromised patients. Gram-positive cocci in clusters = Staphylococci. Gram-negative rods = Pseudomonas (ecthyma gangrenosum). Streptococcus pyogenes also causes NF but is Gram-positive cocci in chains.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT for 6 months develops sudden facial nerve palsy with edematous skin lesions. Slit-skin smear still shows AFB. This is classified as:
opts: Lepra reaction due to inadequate treatment
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction in borderline leprosy patients, presenting with acute nerve function impairment, edema of skin lesions, and may occur during MDT. The key feature is sudden neuritis/nerve palsy. AFB positivity does not mean inadequate treatment if MDT is ongoing.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops oral ulcers, macrocytic anemia, and elevated LFTs. The mechanism of methotrexate toxicity is:
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), depleting tetrahydrofolate needed for purine and thymidylate synthesis. In dermatology, it suppresses rapidly proliferating keratinocytes. Folic acid supplementation reduces mucosal/hepatic toxicity without compromising efficacy.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodulocystic lesions on the face and trunk. He is started on isotretinoin. The most important counseling point before initiating therapy in a female patient of childbearing age is:
opts: Mandatory pregnancy testing and two forms of contraception
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Female patients require a negative pregnancy test before initiation, monthly pregnancy tests during therapy, and two forms of contraception starting 1 month before to 1 month after treatment (iPLEDGE program). This is the most critical counseling point.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male with multiple basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, calcification of the falx cerebri, and odontogenic keratocysts is seen. The gene mutated in this condition encodes:
questions.exp: Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome) is caused by mutations in PTCH1, a tumor suppressor in the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Features include multiple BCCs, odontogenic keratocysts, calcified falx cerebri, palmar/plantar pits, and skeletal anomalies.

questions.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive man develops multiple violaceous papules and plaques on the trunk, hard palate, and lower limbs. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. The causative herpesvirus is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus/KSHV). It is strongly associated with HIV infection. Histopathology shows spindle cell proliferation forming slit-like spaces filled with RBCs, hemosiderin deposits, and plasma cells.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, frozen sections are used primarily to:
opts: Map and examine 100% of the tumor margin
questions.exp: Mohs surgery involves sequential horizontal (en face) frozen section processing, allowing examination of 100% of the surgical margin (unlike conventional bread-loaf sectioning which samples <1%). This maximizes tumor-free margin identification while preserving normal tissue.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with target lesions on the palms and soles, erosions of the oral mucosa, and conjunctival involvement after starting co-trimoxazole. The pathophysiology involves:
opts: Drug-specific T cell activation with keratinocyte apoptosis via Fas-FasL
Immune complex deposition in dermal vessels
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN involves drug-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+) that recognize drug-hapten complexes on keratinocytes, triggering apoptosis via Fas-FasL interaction and granzyme B/perforin pathway. Sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole) are a classic trigger.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with butterfly-shaped facial erythema, photosensitivity, arthralgia, and oral ulcers has a positive ANA (1:640, homogeneous pattern). The most specific antibody for this condition is:
questions.exp: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (~30% sensitivity but ~99% specificity). Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjögren's.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient with a long-standing hyperpigmented plaque on the shin develops an ulcer within it. Biopsy of the ulcer edge shows malignant squamous cells. This type of squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or scar is called:
questions.exp: Marjolin's ulcer is a well-differentiated SCC arising in areas of chronic inflammation, burns, scars, or chronic ulcers (e.g., venous ulcers). It is notorious for painlessness (due to destruction of nerve endings), slow growth, and high metastatic potential despite well-differentiated histology.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child develops oozing, crusted lesions around the mouth and nares with golden-yellow ('honey-colored') crusts. Culture grows coagulase-positive cocci. The first-line treatment for localized impetigo is:
opts: Topical fusidic acid cream with oral cefalexin
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus is treated with topical mupirocin 2% (or retapamulin) for localized disease. Oral antibiotics (cefalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate) are reserved for extensive disease, bullous impetigo, or immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spirochetes. The drug of choice for this patient is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) — chancre on glans penis with positive dark-field microscopy. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the drug of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis. Doxycycline is used for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with periorbital heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules on MCPs/PIPs, and proximal muscle weakness with elevated CK. The most useful investigation to confirm myositis and guide biopsy site is:
questions.exp: In dermatomyositis, MRI (STIR sequences) of affected muscles demonstrates inflammatory edema and helps identify the most active area for targeted biopsy, increasing diagnostic yield. EMG shows myopathic pattern but is non-specific. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with a rash described as 'dewdrops on a rose petal' — vesicles on erythematous bases in crops, sparing palms and soles. He is febrile. The correct statement about the causative virus is:
opts: Establishes latency in dorsal root ganglia and reactivates as herpes zoster
Is a DNA virus belonging to the Retroviridae family
questions.exp: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV, HHV-3) causes chickenpox as primary infection and establishes latency in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia. Reactivation causes herpes zoster. VZV is a DNA virus (Herpesviridae), can cross the placenta (congenital varicella), and immunity is lifelong.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with pruritic papulovesicles symmetrically over elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae. The associated systemic condition is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is pathognomonic of celiac disease — granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips on DIF. Dietary gluten sensitivity triggers anti-endomysial/anti-tTG antibodies. Gluten-free diet improves both skin and gut disease. Dapsone is used for rapid symptom control.

questions.q: A 55-year-old patient presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose with a central ulcer ('rodent ulcer'). The treatment with the highest cure rate for a primary BCC on the nose is:
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery has the highest cure rate for BCC (99% for primary, 95% for recurrent), especially at high-risk sites (nose, periocular, ear). It provides margin-controlled excision while preserving normal tissue, making it ideal for cosmetically sensitive areas.

questions.q: A 35-year-old nurse develops vesicles on her finger after contact with a patient's herpetic lesion. The lesion is painful, tense, and non-umbilicated, located on the finger pulp. This condition is called:
questions.exp: Herpetic whitlow is HSV infection of the finger (usually HSV-1 in children/healthcare workers due to oral contact, HSV-2 in adults via genital contact). It presents as tense, painful vesicles on the finger pad. Unlike felon (bacterial), it is treated with acyclovir and should not be incised.

questions.q: A 28-year-old on dapsone for leprosy develops pallor, fatigue, and cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen. Blood gas shows normal PaO2 with low oxygen saturation. The diagnosis and antidote are:
questions.exp: Dapsone is the most common drug causing methemoglobinemia — oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in hemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. Classic clue: cyanosis with normal PaO2 (pulse oximetry reads ~85%). Treatment: methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV, which reduces MetHb via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase.

questions.q: The Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon is characteristically seen in which of the following conditions?
opts: Acne vulgaris, rosacea, and perioral dermatitis
questions.exp: Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response) — new lesions appearing at sites of trauma — is classic in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Other conditions include warts, molluscum, and lichen nitidus. It reflects disease-specific epidermal/dermal reactivity to trauma.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented macules with loss of sensation in one lesion. Slit-skin smear is negative. Nerve biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells. The bacterial load (BI) is 0. This is classified as:
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum shows strong cell-mediated immunity — well-defined hypopigmented macules with anaesthesia, negative SSS (BI=0), and epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells on biopsy. PB-MDT (6 months: rifampicin + dapsone) is the treatment.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with widespread erythema, weeping, and intense pruritus involving the flexures, and a history of childhood asthma and allergic rhinitis. Her serum IgE is elevated. The primary defect in this condition involves:
opts: Filaggrin gene mutation leading to epidermal barrier dysfunction
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis pathogenesis begins with filaggrin (FLG) gene mutations causing defective epidermal barrier, allowing allergen penetration and sensitization. This triggers Th2-predominant immune response (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31) with elevated IgE. Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) targets this pathway.
